newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PHILIP MORRIS AUSTRALIA LOSES A$1 MLN A DAY.
newsitem.headline: PHILIP MORRIS AUSTRALIA LOSES A$1 MLN A DAY.

text.p: Philip Morris Cos Inc's Australian unit said on Friday it had suspended sales of its cigarettes to wholesalers and retailers because of uncertainty over the replacement of state taxes with federal taxes.
A Phillip Morris Australia spokeswoman told Reuters there was no immediate end to the suspension in sight and it was costing the company A$1 million a day in lost gross margins.
The federal tax designed to replace state taxes ruled out by a High Court decision this week would raise an extra A$500 million a year in government revenues, she said.
"The new excise raised represents a tax increase of A$500 million, which represents three times the industry's profits," Philip Morris spokeswoman Nerida White said.
"Every day without sales costs us A$1 million in gross margin and costs the Commonwealth (federal government) A$10 million in revenue that otherwise would have been collected," she said.
Australia's tobacco companies, including Philip Morris, W.D. & H.O. Wills Ltd and Rothmans Holdings Ltd, had sought urgent discussions with Treasurer Peter Costello, White said.

The High Court ruled on Tuesday that the franchise fees charged by Australia's states and territories on alcohol, tobacco and petrol were in fact excises, which only the federal government is allowed to raise under the constitution.
Treasurer Peter Costello announced on Wednesday the federal government had agreed to the states' request to replace these now unconstitutional excises with federal excises.

Costello said the federal government's duty on petrol would rise 8.1 cents a litre and its excise on tobacco would rise A$167 a kilogram to A$251.27 a kilogram. He said the wholesale sales tax on alcohol would rise by 15 percentage points.

Costello said he had only agreed to impose the new Federal taxes after receiving assurances from the states that they they would refund any extra revenues collected so they did not receive any net new funding and so that prices did not rise.
But White said the tobacco companies could not continue selling their products to retailers and wholesalers while they did not have assurances from the states that the money would be refunded.
She said some of the states had promised to use some of the higher tobacco taxes to push prices down for other products that were taxed like petrol and beer.

"It seems extraordinary to me that smokers should be made to subsidise bottle shops so they can offer discounted beer," White said. She said Philip Morris would look at its suspension on a day-by-day basis.
"The decision by Philip Morris to suspend sales will at least postpone price increases for consumers," she said.
Philip Morris was considering its suspension on a day-by-day basis, but retailers stocks were likely to start running out from Monday.
Philip Morris sells the Peter Jackson, Long Beach and Marlboro brands in Australia and has a market share of about 38 or 39 percent.
Competitor W.D. & H.O. Wills suspended sales to wholesalers from Thursday morning for two days and trading in its shares were halted on Thursday.
Rothmans Holdings Ltd also said it suspended sales on Thursday, but had resumed selling to wholesalers and retailers earlier on Friday.

Rothmans corporate affairs director Peter Alexander said industry representatives would meet with Treasury officials on Friday afternoon and press for a return to the status quo before Tuesday. Without that change back to the old situation, prices would have to rise, he said.
"We've had discussions with the states and they are unable to guarantee us any rebates to fix this situation," Alexander said.
"We can't continue to do business in a climate of uncertainty like this," he said.
Rothmans sells the Winfield, Holiday and Dunhill brands.
Wills' shares were up two cents at A$2.02 on low volume and Rothmans' shares were unchanged at A$7.85 by 11.30 a.m. (0130 GMT).
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
